newsitem.title: SPAIN: Rojo talks up Spain's single currency chances.
newsitem.headline: Rojo talks up Spain's single currency chances.

text.p: Bank of Spain Governor Luis Angel Rojo, in his loudest call yet for participation in Europe's single currency launch, said on Thursday Spain could aspire to being ready at its 1999 start.

"The economic situation is fairly favourable. Spain is situated in such a way that it can reasonably aspire to form part of monetary union in the first phase," Rojo said at a seminar on the Spanish economy.

Spain's five-month-old minority government has grown increasingly shrill in recent days in its demands for recognition of its fiscal efforts, afraid it might be lumped with what is seen as a less credible contender, Italy.

But at a two-day Franco-Spanish summit earlier this week, Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar appeared to win over French President Jacques Chirac who said he had no doubt of Spain's chances but expressed far less conviction over Italy.
Rojo, too, has apparently turned more positive. Up to now, he had focused on urging the government to construct an austere budget - and to stick to these policies in the future.

But his comments on Thursday suggested a change of tack following the government's late September presentation of its 1997 budget draft, which the Bank of Spain greeted with its sixth interest rate cut of the year.

"The improvement in inflation and the firm commitment of budget policy to public deficit reduction are the main points that will help the economy recover in the next few months and advance toward the expected levels on the order of 2.7 percent or something similar next year," Rojo said.
Spain must meet criteria on inflation, long-term interest rates, currency stability, the deficit and debt.

On Wednesday, the European Commission forecast Spain would meet the deficit to GDP criteria of three percent, and said debt would be above 60 percent of GDP at 67.1 percent but that it would head in the right direction.

In its covergence report, the European Monetary Institute (EMI), the precursor of the European central bank, said the peseta had remained stable and that Spain had made progress on inflation and long-term interest rates.

"Nevertheless, strong and sustained action is required as inflation and long-term interest rates remain above their respective reference values, the government deficit-to-GDP ratio, although falling in 1996, is still high and the debt-to-GDP ratio has continued to increase," the EMI said.
